edits.name: Email me this: a long answer sent to the asker's own inbox
edits.description: A parent texts 'email me this' and the long answer, table or plan lands in that parent's own inbox as plain text; either parent can ask. The only address the send tool accepts is the asker's own: a check in code blocks every other send, and blocks when the check itself fails.
edits.example: Jordan texts: 'Email me that comparison.' The full text arrives in her own inbox as plain text from Happy's address. A send that names anyone else on the To, cc or bcc line, or that goes out as a reply-all, is blocked.
edits.how: One shared mail-out server on the host: gog run as an MCP server for the sending address with its write and Gmail-send flags and only `gmail_send_message` registered, signed in with a send-only grant if the installed gog offers one. It is allowed by name on each parent's own agent, denied on the mail readers and every shared agent, and has its own firewall rule (Google only). The card adds one rule to the house-rules plugin, the send-to-owner rule: a send is blocked unless the caller is a parent's own agent and the one recipient is that agent's owner, read from the family file, with no cc, bcc, reply or reply-all target, send-as alias or HTML body. The check fails closed. Before go-live: T5's send-tool turn, then the roadmap's five seeded ways to change the recipient (the other parent and a reply-all among them) and an injected web page. No send cap.

The house-rules plugin: this card adds its send-to-owner rule, and creates the plugin itself if no earlier card has (timed reminders, F007, is the likely first)

The outbound gate that is built before web reading (the gate F019 waits for): the firewall blocking every program by default and the outbound proxy; the roadmap puts the send-to-owner test in that same gate

caveats: The promise that nobody else can be a recipient rests on one in-house rule, and it is not yet shown that the check sees every field that can set a recipient: to, cc and bcc, and also the reply fields, because the upstream page for the mail tool says a send needs 'recipients or a reply-all target'. The seeded sends, a reply-all among them, must all be blocked before this goes live.
The check blocks a wrong recipient; it does not correct it, because the docs describe rewriting parameters for host-owned tools only.

Pinning the recipient does not close every way out: the mailed text is often built from research results, and a link in it can carry private text in its address to whoever runs that site once it is clicked. A link is only as trustworthy as the result it came from.
No send cap: a runaway loop could fill the asker's own inbox until someone notices or the agent's spend cap stops it.
Signing Happy's existing Google account in on the Mac mini for sending is a new use of that account. A send-only grant keeps the token from reading that mailbox, if the installed gog supports it.
edits.safety: Each parent's own agent holds private data and reads outside content, so its mail way out is pinned in code: the house-rules plugin blocks any send not addressed to the calling agent's owner alone, and blocks when the check fails. No mail reader or shared agent gets the tool. Plain text only, so no remote image can report back.

edits.name: Scheduled jobs: three safety switches and one short jobs script
edits.description: Before Happy sends its first scheduled text, three scheduler settings go in: a failed job alerts Tony and not the family, runs missed during a power cut are skipped, and script triggers are off. Every scheduled text is then one job created by one short checked-in script, with its owner's handle read from the family file, a time limit, a tool list, its own daytime hour and its rules in its own message. A job with nothing to say sends nothing.
edits.example: Jordan's 07:00 mail text fails twice in a row: Tony gets one text from Happy saying so and one more when it recovers, and she is not sent the error. After a power cut the 07:00 text does not turn up at 11:40. To quieten a text, Tony switches that one job off.
edits.how: Config first: `cron.failureAlert` with Tony's handle as its destination, `cron.skipMissedJobs: true`, `cron.triggers.enabled: false`. Then test T3: happy-inspect gains one read-only line, `automations list --all --json`, and one throwaway job is added twice under the same `--declaration-key` with a changed message; one job afterwards means one add line per job, two means a name-keyed comparison is kept. Then one short checked-in jobs script, applied through the deploy path as the happy user. Every `automations add` carries `--agent`, `--to` (the owner's handle read from family.json5, never typed in), `--tz`, `--timeout-seconds` and `--announce`. A job that calls the model also carries an explicit `--tools` list and no `--light-context`, so the hard rules load on every run; its message holds its rules: begin with the job's label, answer `NO_REPLY` when there is nothing to say. A text that needs no model is a `--command-argv` job. Something for both parents is two jobs, one each.
depends_on: happy-deploy and happy-inspect (exist): the only two scripts Tony's account may run as the happy user
family.json5 (exists): each job's owner handle is read from it
T3 is run first, to show that the deploy path can list the scheduler's jobs. If it cannot, the jobs script is run by hand in the happy session, as M1 did for plugin installs
Tony provides the daytime hour of each scheduled text at execution of that text's own card, where he has not chosen it already (chosen: 07:00 for the mail text, 21:00 Eastern for the evening text)
caveats: Failed-job alerts reach Tony as an iMessage from Happy, a deliberate exception to his 'alerts by ntfy' decision: OpenClaw's chat notice carries only a tidied cause, while its webhook would post the raw error text to an outside push service. If iMessage itself is down, the existing Grafana alerts still reach him by ntfy.

Alerts start after 2 failures in a row with a 1-hour cooldown. A recurring job is switched off after 10 failures in a row and then disappears from the default job list, which is why the inspect line lists every job, disabled ones included. Without a time limit of its own a model job is bounded only by a 60-minute watchdog, so the script sets one on every job.

Switching script triggers off does not stop the no-model jobs that other cards add through this script: OpenClaw's docs list a command job as a separate kind from the script payloads, condition triggers and stream schedules that the switch turns off.

After a reboot with FileVault locked nothing fires and nothing alerts; the healthchecks dead-man switch stays the only signal for a Mac that is off. One-off reminders still catch up after an outage even with missed runs skipped.

Given up with this form: per-person on and off switches in the family file, automatic clean-up of jobs that no longer match it, and any enforced daily cap or quiet hours. A changed job is edited by hand until an edit step is written; to quieten Happy, Tony switches a job off or a parent silences the thread on the phone. The comparing generator comes back when the script holds more jobs than can be read at a glance.

Reminders Tony sets in chat (F007) are jobs outside the script; the inspect listing shows them beside the scripted ones. The script creates Jordan's jobs too, so her scheduled texts need no command right of her own.
edits.safety: Only restrictive. Script triggers are off before any agent holds the scheduling tool, because they would run with the owning agent's full tool policy. Every job's text goes to its owner alone, whose handle the script reads from the family file; each job has a time limit, and a model job a tool list. Failure alerts go to Tony, not into another person's thread.
unverified: T3: whether a command run as the happy user through the deploy path reaches the scheduler's job list at all; job changes need the admin operator scope, and nothing in Tony's account calls the Gateway today except the two installed scripts.
T3: whether adding a job twice under the same `--declaration-key` updates it or doubles it; the flag was read in the installed code, is not described on the CLI doc page, and nothing was run.
That the first text Happy sends by itself is delivered on this version: M1's sign-off records that replies needed a workaround, so T3's throwaway job also announces one fixed line to Tony.
That a job answering `NO_REPLY` sends nothing and raises no failure alert on iMessage: documented, not tried.

That a failed job of Jordan's alerts Tony and nobody else once the global destination is set (the documented route order, not tried), and where the auto-disable notice lands: the docs say the owning agent receives it even when failure alerts are off, so it may reach the family member's thread and not Tony's.

edits.name: Weather by the hour: the hourly forecast for home
edits.description: Ask whether it will rain at home on Saturday morning and get the chance of rain hour by hour, with any active weather alert for home, straight from the National Weather Service. The evening text and the day-out planner use the same hourly line.
edits.example: Jordan texts: 'Will it rain at home on Saturday between 9 and noon?' Happy answers with the hourly chance of rain for those hours and any active alert for home.
edits.how: Extend the in-house home_weather plugin: follow `forecastHourly` from the points lookup the tool already makes, so the tool can also answer hour by hour, on the same pinned host (api.weather.gov), with the same refusal of redirects and of any forecast address on another host. Active alerts are already fetched with every forecast and stay as they are. Not built: a snowfall figure from the raw gridpoint endpoint, and an alert id in the output. The plugin's own tests are extended with a recorded hourly response, and one live question about rain on a given afternoon is answered by the hour before it goes live.
caveats: Apple's Weather app can already send a notification when rain or snow is about to start or stop, and for government-issued severe-weather alerts at a saved location; Apple notes this is not offered in every country or region. This tool earns its place as the hourly rain line for the evening text (F014) and the day-out planner (F028), and for questions asked inside a Happy conversation.
The National Weather Service hourly forecast reaches seven days ahead, so a question about a day further out gets no hour-by-hour answer until the date comes into range.
The tool knows only the home point, so it cannot answer for a field or a venue somewhere else; for other places Happy falls back to web search.

No snowfall amount in numbers on day one. The field exists in the raw gridpoint data, in millimetres over mostly six-hour intervals, so it would not give an hour-by-hour amount; the forecaster's own text for each period still comes through. It is added only if a first snow forecast shows the need.
edits.safety: Read-only public data from one pinned government host. A lookup sends the home's coordinates and the header that identifies the app, as the National Weather Service asks, and nothing else about the family. What comes back is outside content from a single government source; the tool only reads, and cannot write anything or message anyone.
unverified: What a live hourly response for the home point looks like: the sources cite the weather service's documentation, not a response read for home. The go-live check (one live question about rain on a given afternoon, answered by the hour) settles it.
NWS publishes no numeric rate limit, so the 10-minute cache is a design choice rather than an NWS rule.
Whether Apple's Weather notifications are offered and switched on for the home location on each parent's iPhone: the Apple page read was the Mac Weather guide, and the iPhone guide did not render.
